On my last blog post, I talked about AI as a broad term, what it represents in everybody's mind and what it really is in the inside.

Today, I want to correlate AI, Large Language Models (LLM), Machine Learning (ML), Deep Learning (DL), Neural Networks (NN) and other big words to give you all a better understanding of each concept and how they relate to each other.

Just a quick reminder: the opinions expressed here are stricly my own. They do not represent the opinions or views of my current employer nor any of my previous ones.

Context Is Key​

In 2019, lots of people came together and wrote Artificial Intelligence in the Management of Glioma: Era of Personalized Medicine in which they described "the relationship between the most common AI methods in medicine". Later, in 2023, Pan Singh Dhoni described "the relationship between AI, Machine Learning and Deep Learning" in his research titled Exploring the Synergy between Generative AI, Data and Analytics in the Modern Age.

Both described Artificial Intelligence as a set containing all kind of other subsets (in the mathematical sense of it), like Machine Learning, Deep Learning and Neural Network.

Thanks to complementary studies like Large language models: a primer and gastroenterology applications (2024) and Artificial Intelligence in Emergency Medicine: A Primer for the Nonexpert (2025), more terminology terms could be added to similar schemas, such as Generative AI (GenAI) and Large Language Models (LLM).

Taking into account all their work, we can draw the following AI Taxonomy which pretty much explains the relationship between each. I will use it as a base in this article.

Artificial Intelligence (AI)​

AI is not new, as stated in my previous blog post. At its core, AI really is just about enabling machines to perform tasks requiring a certain level of intelligence.

Machine Learning (ML)​

Zooming in, there is this big subset called Machine Learning.

In the late 80s, general belief was that building an "intelligent behaviour" could be achieved by explicitly writing down logical rules and knowledge (bunch of if-else stating how to act in certain conditions). One programming language that perfectly fits that conviction is Prolog: a declarative programming language based on a set of facts, rules and relations and where a computation takes the form of a query.

However, the limitations are increasingly evident: encoding knowledge by hand is labor-intensive and an ever-ending task. This is where Machine Learning come in. As knowledge-based systems disappointed by their lack of generalization of knowledge, studies on more automated learning techniques started to emerge, especially thanks to new algorithms development like Bayesian inference and Iterative Dichotomiser 3. Instead of experts providing domain rules, we provide labeled data and let the algorithm infer the rules (training phase). This inverted the knowledge acquisition problem! Data-driven AI was born.

Machine Learning systems are thus systems fed with data that use algorithms to recognize patterns and infer rules from it. Its most important phase is the "learning" part, where the algorithms would improve their performance on a task through data: the more data, the better output accuracy in the end.

Neural Networks (NN)​

While studies on ML systems were going great, other forms of AI computation were researched to fulfill gaps in many domains like vision or natural language understanding, as those tasks were proved hard to define or infer rules from dataset.

Indeed, to train an ML system, you'd have to go through the dataset to label the information. In the end, you still depend on humans selecting useful features to train the system (e.g. to recognize a cat in an image, you might require manually designed features representing paws, whiskers, ears and so on...).

Artificial Neural Network (ANN)​

Researchers tried to teach the systems pattern recognition from the training data. They mimicked the human brain's model for information processing and created Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs).

An artificial neural network is a computational model composed of interconnected artificial neurons (typically organized in layers) that transforms inputs into outputs. An artificial neuron is actually a highly simplified mathematical abstraction that combines several input values with adjustable weights, adds a bias and applies an activation function.

If you read that out loud, it does not even help to understand it, right? Well, let me give you an example to simplify it. Imagine that we want to predict whether a student will pass an exam based on three factors:

  1. hours studied (how long the student prepared the exam)
  2. hours slept (how much sleep did they get the night before)
  3. attendance (the percentage of classes attended)

Instead of manually defining rules, we train an ANN to learn the relationships between these factors and the exam results. To achieve this, we would give it historical data as training dataset:

In order to train the system to learn the patterns and to predict the output value, the ANN will repeatedly:

  • predict whether a student will pass based on actual input values
  • compare its prediction with the actual result
  • calculate the error between them
  • adjust its weights using backpropagation and an optimization algorithm
  • repeat the process across many examples

Over time, it learns useful relationships between study habits, attendance, sleep, and obviously the exam results.

This interactive demonstration uses a fixed mathematical formula, not a trained neural network. It illustrates how changing inputs can change a model's output.

What's impressive is not simply predicting the outcome (especially in this context where the formula is quite simple), it's more about how the prediction is learned! An ANN learns numerical weights and combinations of inputs from examples. Using backpropagation, the hidden neurons unlock much richer learning behaviours and thus could discover useful features and encodings of the input domain rather than relying on manually written human-designed rules.

At the time they got developed, however, neural networks were not that fabulous... mainly due to the limits of computational power and the size of available data. Early neural networks established a general principle though: interconnected mathematical units can learn from data. And different tasks required different structures!

  • Images benefit from networks that recognize local spatial patterns.
  • Complex abstractions benefit from networks with many processing layers.
  • Sequences benefit from networks that maintain information across time.

These requirements led to Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs).

ArchitectureMain distinguishing featureTypical strength
CNNLocal filters and weight sharingSpatial patterns
DNNMultiple hidden layers of learned patternsHierarchical representations
RNNRecurrent state across stepsSequential dependencies

Deep Learning (DL)​

DNN and Deep Learning are closely related terms: the first is a model architecture for neural networks based on multiple layers of learned representations to model complex patterns in data ; the second refers to a broader approach of training and using such models.

The power of neural networks comes from scaling them up in depth, width and data, making deep neural networks a go-to approach in AI research: it was setting new records in different tasks such as "image classification, object detection, machine translation, language modelling" (R. Mundlamuri, G. R. Gunnam, N. K. Mysari and J. Pujuri, 2025).

Transformers​

Deep learning significantly improved perception and language processing, but recurrent architectures (RNNs) had important limitations: they process sequences through recurrent steps, making large-scale parallel training difficult. They can also struggle with very long-range dependencies.

For example, imagine a deep RNN reads a story and stumbles across this sentence: The dog chase the ball because it was red. What does the "it" means? The dog? The ball? As a human, you immediately understand that "it" refers to the ball, because balls can be red and the sentence makes sense that way. But how does the computer do that?

To fix this kind of issues, researchers developed attention mechanisms so models could focus selectively on relevant parts of an input. This led to the Transformer architecture.

Older neural networks, like RNNs, process words one after another, passing information along as they go. A Transformer does something different: it allows every word to look at other words and decide which ones matter most. This process is called "self-attention": it helps the transformer calculates how strongly different words should influence one another.

Transformers are thus deep neural network architectures built around attention mechanisms, especially self-attention. They replace recurrent processing with attention-based computation, making training more parallelizable.

Generative AI (GenAI)​

Up to now, we talked about a lot of systems that are able to predict an output value based on input values. These are what we call classifiers, they are used to predict a category based on the values received as input.

GenAI refers to AI systems that also learn patterns or distributions from data but they use them to generate new content such as text, image, audio, video, code and structured information. Unlike classifiers, a generative model produces an output resembling or satisfying patterns learned during training.

A few years ago, when you asked Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini or DeepSeek for a random number between 1 and 20, they used to answer 17. How is that random if you ask AI systems and they all give you the same number? (J. Agrawal, 2025).

As generative models predicts what the next word will be, based on their training data, it only takes data where more representations of "generate a random number between 1 and 20" gives "17" to lead to a biased generative model. This is a part of the explanation as to why some AI systems generated contents that were deemed incorrect or inappropriate at times: bias.

However, GenAI are not the only systems that are biased: anything that infers patterns from data will perpetuate reality biases through the learned representations (e.g. classifiers like Microsoft facial recognition services, which had issues identifying women and dark-skinned individuals (Buolamwini & Gebru, 2018)). This is inherent to model training and cannot be avoided. However, it can be mitigated. And mitigation is also a tough job!

Did you know that when Google first released Gemini, they said they designed it as an attempt to avoid perpetuating pre-existing societal prejudices? But in fact, they actually overcompensated the bias, and ended up leaning toward another issue of misrepresentation of "mainstream culture" (Shamim, 2024).

In the end, what are Large Language Models (LLMs) ? Well, it's rather simple: LLMs are a subset of GenAI that are specialized in text generation. Just like MidJourney is a generative AI specialized in image generation, and MusicGen is a generative AI specialized in audio generation, LLMs such as GPT, Gemini, Claude, Mistral or DeepSeek are generative AI specialized in text.

Why is it called like that though?

  • Large: it has a very large number of learned parameters, sometimes billions or more. These numerical values help encode patterns learned during training.
  • Language: it is trained to process language: words, sentences, conversations, and other text-based information, including programming languages.
  • Model: it is a mathematical system that learns statistical patterns and uses them to make predictions.

Thus, an LLM is a deep-learning system built on the Transformer Architecture, trained on massive text datasets to understand, generate, and reason about human language. It learns by predicting the next token in a sequence repeated trillions of times across terabytes of data.

I have yet to talk about what tokens are, so stay tuned... this will be for the next article!

What are LLMs' limitations, evolution and future through model iterations ?​

In the past years, LLMs have evolved from relatively simple text-prediction systems into models capable of writing softwares, analyzing documents, solving mathematical problems, processing images and interacting with external tools (via "connectors").

However, being able to generate convincing answers is not the same as

  1. being accurate,
  2. being reliable, and
  3. being capable of understanding every situation.

Evolution​

LLMs will undoubtedly continue to grow and become more performant. We already witness significant improvements with each new model iteration, from better language understanding to enhanced reasoning capabilities.

Hence even developers say things like "the AI writes better code than us".

What drives their evolution is:

  • scale (by increasing the amount of training data, parameters and computational power) ;
  • capabilities (by creating more connectors to move beyond text generation (e.g. multimodality, extensive reasoning, etc.)) ;
  • reliability (by improving factual accuracy, verification and efficiency - especially in code generation).

Evolution of Large Language Models

  1. 2017

    Transformers

    The attention-based architecture establishes the foundation for modern LLMs.

    Attention Is All You Need
  2. 2018-2019

    Pretrained language models

    Models learn general language patterns from large datasets and can be adapted to different tasks.

    GPTBERTGPT-2
  3. 2020-2021

    Scaling up

    Larger models demonstrate stronger few-shot learning and broader language capabilities.

    GPT-3
  4. 2022-2023

    Instruction-following and chat

    Post-training makes models more useful for conversations, instructions, and assistance.

    InstructGPTChatGPTGPT-4Llama 2
  5. 2023-2024

    Multimodality and longer context

    Models increasingly process images, audio, and longer inputs alongside text.

    GPT-4oGemini 1.5Claude 3
  6. 2024-2025

    Reasoning and tool use

    Models increasingly use additional computation for difficult problems and interact with external tools.

    o1o3DeepSeek-R1
  7. 2025-2026

    More capable AI systems

    Progress combines stronger reasoning, efficient inference, multimodal interaction, and agentic workflows.

    GPTClaudeGeminiQwen

Limitations​

You might already have used AI and you already found out about a few of its limitations. You can find a non-exhaustive list in the table below.

LimitationExplanationExample
HallucinationsModels can generate plausible but incorrect informationInventing a scientific citation or a nonexistent API method
Limited knowledge freshnessTraining knowledge can become outdatedDescribing an obsolete software API as current
Context limitationsModels can miss, forget, or misinterpret information in long conversations or documentsOverlooking a requirement in a 200-page specification
BiasModels can reproduce biases present in training data or introduced by optimizationProducing different recommendations based on demographic cues
Non-determinismResponses can vary across runs, even with similar inputsGenerating different solutions to the same programming problem
Weak factual groundingModels do not inherently verify every statement against reliable evidenceGiving a confident but unsupported historical explanation
Computational costTraining and serving large models require substantial hardware, electricity, and infrastructureExpensive inference for millions of requests
Limited real-world understandingText-based learning does not automatically provide reliable physical or situational understandingSuggesting an impractical mechanical solution

Future​

The future of LLMs and the frontier models in a generic point of view may be the transition from models that generate answers to systems that can plan, act, check their work and collaborate with people.

This includes:

  • native multimodal handling (integrate text, images, audio, video and potentially sensor information at some point to enrich the LLMs representations of the world - part of this is already the case) ;
  • more deliberate reasoning (extract computation allocated for difficult tasks, exploring alternative solutions, checking intermediate results, etc.) ;
  • more capable agents (instead of explaining how to perform a task, it could carry out multi-step workflows using tools, with checkpoints, permissions and human supervision - we already see that in the IT sphere where developers are now becoming AI-produced code reviewers... but this will be for another article as well!) ;
  • better factual verification (rather than producing a plausible answer, they can fact-check it) ;
  • better long-term context and memory (persist information more effectively, maintain coherence across lengthy conversations, etc.).

What you see coming for the future of LLMs is a shift towards more integrated, capable, and reliable systems that can interact with the world in a more human-like manner, reason more effectively, and maintain long-term memory of specific usecases.

Conclusion​

In the end, we talked about the whole history behind LLMs and what they really are. We also mentioned their limits, their evolution and what we can see coming for the future.

Next up for this series is what exactly tokens are! Hopefully a short article, for once 😉

But let me ask you a sincere question: what are your thoughts on the future of LLMs?

Stay up to date, subscribe to my newsletter!

There's a lot of talk about Artificial Intelligence (AI) and how it currently is changing the world as we know it. It is true that AI is shaping a new future for us, but it is also true that AI is not as much of a threat as the car was back in the day, or as the industrial revolution was.

I feel like it is mandatory to talk about AI through different lenses, and not just through the lens of software development, which is the field I am most familiar with.

Just a quick reminder: the opinions expressed here are stricly my own. They do not represent the opinions or views of my current employer nor any of my previous ones.

To grasp its full impact and to have a more holistic view of the AI technology and what it represents, we need to talk about it from different perspectives, such as:

  • what is AI? Definitions through etymology, social representation, research studies and mathematical concepts
  • what are LLMs, and how do they work? What are their limitations, their evolution and their future through model iterations?
  • the current AI models and their comparison
  • what is vibe coding, and how does it relate to AI?
  • intelligence, bias, trust, sustainability, accountability
  • the impact of AI (in our political landscapes, in our economic landscapes, in our education systems, in our social lives, in our careers - and especially in software development, on our mental health, on our creativity, on our future, ...)

In this blog post series, I want to talk about how AI is changing the way we work and live, its impact on our social lives and career choices, and how we can adapt to this new reality. It is not meant to be an exhaustive analysis of all these topics, but rather an attempt to reflect and have a debate about the future we are heading to.

To understand what is Artificial Intelligence, I believe it is important to understand what we mean by "intelligence", and why "artificial intelligence" means much more than buzzwords.

Intelligence​

The term intelligence comes from the Latin word intelligere, which means "to comprehend, perceive".

The concept of intelligence has been studied for a long time, and did undergo some sort of evolution from a unitary concept to a more complex multidimensional one (meaning we had one definition because we thought there was only one "intelligence" but there are actually plenty so we enlarged our scope and gave more definitions).

Some remarkably important definitions and their authors:

  • A. Binet would define intelligence as "the ability to judge, understand and reason effectively".
  • R. Cattell distinguishes between fluid intelligence (problem-solving ability) and crystallized intelligence (acquired knowledge).
  • H. Gardner talks about it being "the capacity to solve problems or create products valued in a culture".
  • R. Sternberg defines it as "the ability to achieve success by adapting to, shaping, and selecting environments; includes analytical, creative and practical intelligence".
  • There are also some studies that highlights the definition of emotional intelligence as "the ability to recognize, understand, and manage emotions in oneself and others" (D. Goleman) or "[...] involves perceiving, using, understanding, and regulating emotions" (P. Salovey and J.D. Mayer).
  • D. Wechsler defines intelligence as "the global capacity to act purposefully, think rationally, and deal effectively with the environment".

All their studies and definitions collectively show the shift from a single conception toward broader adaptive and socio-emotional views of intelligence.

Among these intelligences, we can talk about linguistic intelligence, logical-mathematical intelligence, spatial intelligence, musical intelligence, emotional intelligence, social intelligence, interpersonal and intrapersonal intelligence, and even domain-specific intelligences (e.g. creative, digital, verbal, mathematical, leadership, collaborative, etc.).

Artificial​

The term artificial comes from the Latin word artificialis, which mean "made with art". This Latin term was formed by the contraction of two roots, ars which means "art", and facere which means "to do, make".

Originally, it refers to anything made, produced, or done by human beings as opposed to what is naturally occurring. It nowadays broadly spans to everyday manufactured goods, synthetic materials and modern technology.

Artificial Intelligence​

In regards to what these buzzwords trigger in every human's mind, well... this is complex as it means different things contextually and dependently of the person's culture and background.

In the 1960s and 70s, Non-Playable Characters (NPCs) emerged in video games and evolved to become rich lifelike companions found in modern gaming. These were referred to as "AI", back then.

In the 1990s, search/query engines and apps like google.com were referred to as "AI". The same fact goes with automated machine translations, or route planning (GPS) at some point.

Later on, voice assistants like Apple's Siri (2011), Window's Cortana (2014), Amazon's Alexa (2014), Google's Assistant (2016), ... were labelled as such.

In 2022 and later, ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Grok, DeepSeek, Perplexity and others are now considered "AI".

In this 21st century, any kind of algorithm performing deemed-complex actions might actually be defined as AI (chess player, robots behaviour, self-driving vehicules, ...). That is what it means, to become a buzzword...

Measuring Intelligence​

The first way of measuring intelligence was the Turing test: "if the interrogator cannot distinguish the human from the machine, solely on the basis of their answers to questions, then the machine can be assumed intelligent". It basically measures a machine's ability to exhibit intelligent human-like behaviour to the point where a human evaluator cannot distinguish the machine from the human.

Apart from the fact that the Turing test also assesses the judge and promotes imitators, the main problem with it is that it focuses too much on human behaviour. It evaluates "acting like a human". This is one of the four foundational pillars of artificial intelligence and cognitive modelling outlined in S. Russell and P. Norvig's book named "Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach".

Schools of Thought​

1. Thinking as a Human - Cognitive Modelling​

[The automation of] activities that we associate with human thinking, activities such as decision-making, problem solving, learning... (Bellman, 1978)

The goal is to build machines that mimic the inner working of human mind. It requires using cognitive science and introspection to figure out how human solve problems, learn and perceive the world, to build a computational model of human reasoning so the machine's thought process mirrors human psychology.

2. Thinking Rationally - The Laws Of Thoughts​

The study of the computations that make it possible to perceive, reason, and act (Winston, 1992).

The goal is to build systems based strictly on irrefutable logic and formal mathematical laws. It traces back to Aristotle's syllogisms (if A=B and B=C, then A=C). The built machines use formal notation and logic to make foolproof inferences.

However, this is hardly applicable into the real world: human beings are far from perfect flawless maths, they are messy contradictory beings.

3. Acting as a Human - The Turing Test​

The study of how to make computers do things at which, at the moment, people are better (Rich and Knight, 1991).

The goal is to build machines that behave exactly as a person would, to the point where it is indistinguishable (as mentioned earlier). It focuses on entirely observable interactions.

4. Acting Rationally - The Rational Agent​

The study of the design of intelligent agents (Poole et al., 1998).

The goal is to "do the right thing" to achieve a specific goal. It uses computational intelligence to design software agents that operate autonomously to maximize their chances of success in achieving their set goal.

An agent (from Latin term agere which means "to do, act, drive") is just an algorithm that acts. Beware that all computer programs are designed to do something, but agents are expected to operate autonomously, perceiving their environment, adapting to changes, pursuing their set goal.

Instead of trying to mimic every nuance of a human brain or figure out every logical law, the agent simply takes actions designed to optimize its performance (using probability, by learning when doing trial-and-errors then adapting itself to maximize their gain and get closer to their goal).

AI as Rational Agents​

While the ideal system would be one that fluidly combines all four, modern AI systems generally prioritize acting rationally, a decision made unanimously across industries for several core reasons:

  1. goal-oriented efficiency: rational agents are designed to maximize performance measures - by quantifying outcomes, they consistently choose the path that yields the best results with the lowest cost.
  2. adaptability and robustness: rather than following rigid rules, they learn from their environment, adjust their behaviours to adapt to changing conditions and new data.
  3. predictability and consistency: because their actions are guided by logical reasoning rather than emotion or bias, their decision-making is predictable and reliable.

It is deemed the best approach among the four, because it has the capacity to balance between perfectly mimicking human flaws and using strict, rigid logical paths.

Rational Agent?​

Rational (from Latin rationalis, which means "reasonable, logical" derived from ratio, "reckoning, calculation, reason") refers to anything that is logically sound, sane or based on objective thought rather than impulse. In this context, it means achieving the best possible outcome, which assumes the outcome is measurable.

An agent (from Latin agentem, the present participle of agere, translated to "the one doing") can perform any intellectual activity that a human does (win a game of chess, play games, etc.).

Fundamental Issues​

The main problem of AI is not doing the task (e.g. unloading a dishwasher in a lab) but it is to adapt to an environment change in which it has to perform the task itself (unloading a dishwasher in a new home setting).

As humans, we are able to adapt to our environment thanks to our senses (vision through the eyes, hearing through the ears, smell through the nose, taste through the mouth, touch through the skin).

Thanks to our brain, we are also given some really interesting abilities that represent complex issues for AI:

  • representation: store knowledge systematically, find/define relationships
  • search: many tasks can be viewed as searching a very large problem space for a solution
  • inference: facts can be inferred from other facts
  • learning: it is essential in an intelligent system
  • planning: starting with general facts about the world, about the effects of basic actions on the world, etc.

An agent, on the contrary, perceives its environment through sensors and acts upon that environment through effectors. α(t)=f[x(t),x(t−1),...,x(0)]\alpha(t) = f[x(t), x(t-1),...,x(0)]α(t)=f[x(t),x(t−1),...,x(0)] where α\alphaα is the action and xxx the percept (= an observation of the current environment settings perceived by the agent's sensors).

A rational agent does "the right thing", which means that for every possible percept sequence, the rational agent should select the action that is expected to maximize its performance measure (given the evidence provided by the percept sequence and whatever built-in knowledge the agent has).

What is interesting when building a rational agent is that we, as system designers, design that performance measure which ultimately represents its goal.

⚠ Rationality is not optimality. Taking rational decisions depends on the agent's percepts history (up to now) and the expected experiences in the future, not on future percepts nor experiences of others. Optimality is rationality with omniscience! Rationality is about optimizing the expected performance.

How to evaluate outcomes and objectives?​

There are actually three closely related concepts involved here, but they operate at different levels. Let me break them down for you.

Remark

Just a quick note - and I won't go in much details because we could talk about it for hours - but there are several classes of rational agents depending on their level of intelligence: simple reflex agents, model-based agents, goal-based agents, utility-based agents and learning agents.

The two last (utility-based and learning) agents are particularly interesting because they are able to estimate how desirable a state of the environment is, and use that estimation to make decisions under uncertainty.

Utility Function​

The utility function UUU calculates a value from a state θ\thetaθ at time ttt: U(θ(t))U(\theta(t))U(θ(t)). This value represents the benefit the agent has from being in state θ(t)\theta(t)θ(t).

Consider a cleaning robot:

  • one possible state could be all rooms cleaned with 80% battery remaining,
  • another could be only half the rooms cleaned with low battery.

The agent evaluates which future states are preferable and chooses actions that are expected to maximize utility.

The focus of the utility function is therefore the expected long-term desirability of outcomes. It is an internal concept used directly by the agent to make decisions.

Reward Function​

The reward function R(s,a,s′)R(s,a,s')R(s,a,s′) assigns a reward to a transition from state sss to state s′s's′ after taking action aaa.

In the cleaning robot example:

  • cleaning a room may give a reward of +10,
  • bumping into furniture may give -20,
  • consuming too much energy may give -5.

Rewards provide immediate feedback during execution. They help the agent learn which actions tend to produce better outcomes over time.

The focus of the reward function is therefore local or short-term progress. It is typically defined by the environment or the system designer and observed by the agent while it acts.

Performance Measure​

The performance measure is the overall criterion used to evaluate whether the agent successfully accomplished its objective.

For our cleaning robot, the performance measure could include:

  • total cleaning time,
  • energy consumption,
  • percentage of rooms cleaned,
  • number of collisions with furniture.

Unlike the utility function, the performance measure is an external evaluation criterion. It is usually defined by the designer rather than by the agent itself.

Its focus is the final real-world objective. By defining a performance measure, we specify what "success" actually means for the agent.

Utility Function vs Performance Measure​

Both the performance measure and the utility function quantify how well an agent is doing. However, they are different concepts and do not necessarily optimize the exact same thing.

Suppose:

  • the performance measure is the total time required to clean all rooms,
  • while the robot's utility function is the estimated time remaining until every room is clean.

These are different:

  • The performance measure is something external. It is used to judge the robot's final behavior.
  • The utility function is something internal. It helps the robot decide what to do next based on the information available to it at that moment.

In other words:

  • the performance measure tells us how the agent is ultimately evaluated,
  • while the utility function helps the agent choose actions expected to achieve good outcomes.

Both are needed because a rational agent must not only be evaluated according to some objective, but must also have an internal mechanism for selecting actions that are likely to satisfy that objective.

Relationship Between Reward and Utility​

The reward function and the utility function are also closely related, but they are not identical:

  • The reward function provides immediate feedback signals.
  • The utility function evaluates the long-term desirability of outcomes.

In many learning systems, the utility can be viewed as the expected accumulation of future rewards.

For example:

  • receiving +10 for cleaning one room is a short-term reward,
  • but finishing the entire house efficiently without exhausting the battery corresponds to high overall utility.

A rational agent therefore learns to choose actions that may maximize short-term rewards while still leading to the best long-term outcomes.

Conclusion​

To summarize everything we discussed, Artificial Intelligence is not a single unified concept but rather a collection of approaches aimed at building systems capable of performing tasks that we associate with intelligence.

Modern AI system predominantly follow the rational agent approach: they are designed to perceive their environment, evaluate possible actions, and choose the ones most likely to achieve a given objective. To do so, these systems rely on mathematical models, probabilities, utility functions, reward mechanisms and performance measures in order to estimate which actions are expected to produce the best outcomes.

However, AI is not simply about "thinking like humans" or perfectly reproducing human intelligence. In practice, most modern systems are optimized to act efficiently toward measurable goals under uncertainty.

Understanding these foundations is essential if we want to discuss AI seriously, not as a buzzword but as a technological, social, economic and philosophical transformation that is already reshaping the world around us.

And perhaps the most important question is not whether machines can become intelligent, but rather how humans choose to design, use, and coexist with them.

For quite some time now, I have been thinking about my career and how I would like it to evolve. You know that too, don't you? Every time you have an interview as a young person, you are asked "where do you see yourself in x years?". It did not tickle me at the beginning, but with some experience, you learn and understand what you like and especially what you don't like.

Finally, where do I see myself in a few years?

Just a quick reminder: the opinions expressed here are stricly my own. They do not represent the opinions or views of my current employer nor any of my previous ones.

If you know me, you probably know that I have been directing my professional career towards continuous learning (for me and for those in front of me!). In this blog post, I will try to explain why I decided to make that move and where I want to be in the future.

A bit of context​

I have always been eclectic. I like to try new things out and see how I perform (and how I could do better). This is one of the reasons I decided to study Information Technology (IT) in the first place.

In this professional area, learning and sharing knowledge and experience is a must. IT represents an entire world moving faster than any other I know of. Yesterday, you would hire someone to create your website from scratch. Today, you can build it yourself with ChatGPT and other AIs which do most of the job for you. The fact that everything moves so fast and that you can't master every single tech that exists in this world makes it clear:

  • Stop trying to know everything, rely on others and learn from them!
  • Nobody knows everything, let people learn from you!
  • Teamwork makes the difference, believe in others.

Although I praise working in team, we are on the verge of a radical change in our society: there are currently a lot more people with 20-30 years of experience than younger people in the companies and they are not retiring yet. This has two downsides:

  1. These experienced profiles are not always willingly updating their knowledge (and I can understand that they are tired and soon will stop working) nor do they especially like to share with others.
  2. The age difference makes it really hard to connect with newcomers.

Short career but lots of life experiences​

To be honest, I have been in several companies in my career. I wanted to see how green the grass is here and there. And I have always seen the same thing: unique profiles either trying to pull up teams and projects or dooming everyone and everything, slowing down progress and burning money uselessly. Unfortunately for me, it is more like the second scenario. Don't get me wrong though! I love creating. I love teamworking to bring people's solutions to life. And I especially love learning. But after around 3 years of professional work in various organizations, I grew tired of those who do not aim for excellence as I do. I mean, why would you develop a digital solution if it is to do it like crap? All you do is shoot either your future self or one of your fellows who will have to maintain it later on. Which is exactly why I decided to turn tables.

I decided to work on that problem to prevent others from feeling like they try hard for nothing. I wanted to avoid needless burnouts like many before me who grew tired of efforts thrown in waste.

Everything comes to those who wait​

For the past two years, I was looking for a way to increase the value that us developers give to our businesses. But I mainly looked for ways to avoid weariness, exhaustion and overstrain. Indeed, I felt my stress and tiredness levels raising way above average. I could not stand it, but had no idea how to solve the problems I was facing...

Surprisingly to me, in 2021, I got a message from a former teacher. She asked me if I was okay to take some hours at university to sub for a sick colleague. This was the trigger. Coming back to where everything started, where I got taught how to do my job, it made me realize a lot of things!🤩

I had evolved. My experiences in the professional world connected me to knowledge and people. I discovered new ways of working, new ways of thinking and I met my ideal. I understood that I wanted to learn but above all, teach others.

Since then, I have been sharing my knowledge, mindset and how technical excellence can bring happiness in the proper environment. Whether I am doing it for students at the Henallux, or at my clients' in front of colleagues.

That made me realize where I wanted to go... 🚀

Back to the basics​

Have you ever had this feeling that you did not understand the whole concept explained to you during class, training or whatever? Rest assured then, you're not alone! I graduated in 2019. Reading now the same lessons I had back then, what a difference! I now can really see that I improved and learnt a bunch of stuff in a short time. This is really thrilling for the future! 😃

However, it feels quite strange for the 24-year-old me to teach people of my age or sometimes older than I am. And I have to admit that forcing myself to go back to the basics, to understand what I have to teach in order to vulgarize it and share my passion, it genuinely is a growing experience.

When I first took the teacher job, I was not sure about it. I mean, everyone has its share of impostor syndrome to deal with, right? But then, each time I took a new role there, I proved myself wrong. I get into the classroom, do my stuff and everyone goes home happy (except when I give homework😁).

Then you know, I kept thinking... Why is it so difficult to work if there are all that knowledge available and people don't know about it (or don't use it)? I feel like the current professionals, often way older than me, lack of a fundamental element: the mindset. At the Henallux, we don't teach a language or a specific design pattern. We try to teach the students how to continuously improve. It does not matter that you don't know how to do C++, Cobol, NodeJS or Python. It does not matter that you don't know all the details about networking or that you haven't experienced all the operation systems. You can teach yourself!

Teaching professionals?​

When I was working in Luxembourg, I met amazing people I immediatly considered as my mentors (👋 Guillaume Faas & Yoan Thirion). I mean, they had the mindset! 3 days with them were more valuable than 5 weeks spent elsewere in terms of learning. I brought that with me when I came back to Belgium (not them obviously..! the way they share what they know, and why they do it).

Through my current employer, I've been sent to various clients who mainly considered me a developer. But my interest lies in the fact that I could help my clients improve. I started looking for challenging missions where I could be more than a developer, where I could learn from them but teach them too!

Then it happened. I had the incredible chance to bring my expertise in a wonderful walloon startup called Pluriell. This new adventure - my first coaching(-only) mission ever - was extremely positive for this client! And me too! Through many discussions, presentations, custom accompaniements for specific problems, and code katas, I believe it gave them fresh insight, new methodologies, standards and objectives but mostly confidence and knowledge on what they (could) do right and what they (could) do wrong. When it comes to what I learnt from them, apart from broadening my views on how you work in a Belgian startup, I can also say that it brought me more experience and connections as a coach. It also definitely strengthened my will to interact with others, to teach and learn from them. And honestly, backed by experienced professionals like Yoan and Guillaume who kept showing me the way, it felt like a wonderful trip.

In a more recent update of my life, I happened to become a co-organizer of the Software Craftsmanship Luxembourg meetup with Guillaume and Arthur Grailet, for which we meet with other great individuals to share our understandings... I am still learning the ropes, but being part of this community and forced to go out of my comfort zone is really something I missed from being a student.

From dev to teacher & coach​

Being a teacher is one thing. When you have to dive deep into JavaScript or explain how you can write efficient algorithms to people who just recently left their school's bench, it really forces you to reflect. But coaching people way older than you in their own field... this is new!😆

I think that both positions bring me the feeling to be what I think is a real IT consultant: to help people concretely. That obviously includes:

  • to understand how they feel (often simply listen to them),
  • to help them optimize the way they work by pointing out where they can improve,
  • but also by showing them what they already do right! And finally, the most important thing is... to discuss things, give pieces of advice based on the context and bring them new value.

Teaching and coaching... these actions are actually quite close. The idea is to build a story, narrate it and believe that people grasp the morality out of it. If they don't, it is part of the job to attack from another angle in order to bring them what they require to go forward.

I truly like the jobs. You need to understand how people think, and how you can convey the right information (and emotion) to them. You have to master your subject, and if not: be transparent and admit you don't know everything. They don't know either anyway, so you can (and should) just look it up with them so that everyone levels up!

Conclusion​

Sometimes you have to go back to your roots to grow bigger 🌳

I look forward to the surprises life will put next on my way, and I am sure everybody (and especially I) will learn more throughout the journey!

By the way, if you are looking for an Agile Technical Coach, hit me up on LinkedIn.

Stay up to date, subscribe to my newsletter!

I decided to talk about the architecture choice I take when developing my apps!

Just a quick reminder: the opinions expressed here are stricly my own. They do not represent the opinions or views of my current employer nor any of my previous ones.

Not long ago, I have been asked the following by fellow developers:

How do you structure your projects because when they evolve, the basic n-tier architecture becomes more complex and they tend to create messy solutions.

I don't have all the answers but what I actually said is that when it comes to my own projects, I make a simple choice:

  • If I am working on a basic CRUD app, I will definitely go for a 3-Tier architecture.
  • But if I need to build a more complex app requiring a strong business logic and which must scream its goal, I will definitely use what Robert C. Martin called the Clean Architecture in 2012. Of course, my version is not strictly following what Uncle Bob describes in his blog as I have tailored it to my needs but let's talk about it.

Nowadays though, I tend to be more inclined to use the latter. But what does the Clean Architecture bring me that I love and that n-tier does not?

The N-Tier architecture​

What is it?​

First of all, it would be a shame to talk about the Clean Architecture and not talk about what I have learnt during my years at school: the n-tier architecture. This type of architecture is usually presented as and mixed up with one of its specific version: the 3-tier architecture.

This architecture places the data as the core of the application. The 3 layers are:

  1. the presentation layer, responsible of presenting the information to the outside ;
  2. the logic layer, responsible of the business logic that should be applied on the data ;
  3. the data layer, responsible of the data access.

Of course, the "n" in the name means that you can actually have less or more than 3 tiers. The layers described above are just the common ground. There are other types of comparable structures like the 2-tier architecture, the single tier, the 4-tier ... When developing a project, you usually tailor the architecture to your needs. You could even subdivide the 3 common layers into sub-layers depending on your requirements.

Pros & Cons​

For the advantages, we can list the following:

  • more secure — The presentation layer (usually the UI or such) is not "directly" wired to the database. All connections to it are shielded by the logic layer.
  • easily maintainable — at the time of its "creation", this archi allowed the developers to maintain it much more easily than the previous architectures did.
  • easy to reuse — it is easier to reuse the logic of each layer.

For the disadvantages, let's have a quick look too:

  • increase in effort — implementing new features takes time as you have to go through all tiers. Changing a single thing in the database layer is reflected to the logic and presentation layers as they directly rely on it.
  • increase in complexity — when it grows, it becomes more difficult to keep it clean, understandable and predict the impact of a change.
  • harder to test — implementing tests is quite difficult as everything is highly coupled to the layer it points toward.

When to use it?​

In my humble opinion, using the n-tier architecture is a good start when you need to develop the prototype of an idea because you need to showcase something quickly. This will unfortunately tend to make things less great for the future though.

You could also use this archi when you need to build an easy CRUD app. Speaking of such, it is often used when you simply want to query a database. I once did that for one of my employers.

The Clean Architecture​

What is it?​

This architecture puts the Domain at the center, and in charge of everything. It also requires more intentional designs as you do not rely on your database directly. Built with the CQRS pattern, I consider it the best way to write a software with maintainability and simplicity in mind.

Historical fact: the 3-Tiered architecture came in 1992 thanks to John J. Donovan and was followed by others afterwards:

  • Hexagonal Architecture / Ports & Adapters (2005, Alistair Cockburn),
  • Onion Architecture (2008, Jeffrey Palermo),
  • Clean Architecture (2012, Robert C. Martin).

Pros & Cons​

For the advantages, we can list the following:

  • less coupled code, better testability — as the code is less coupled due to using abstractions everywhere you can, you can easily mock dependencies and unit test your components. It also facilitates the development in each layer as they are not highly coupled together, allowing teams to work in parallel on each layer.
  • separation of concerns — the architecture kind of forces you to think about your use cases and dependencies. The UI also does not care about how your database looks, nor does it care about the packages you use to generate a PDF for example...
  • better features exposition
  • better application of SOLID principles
  • better evolutivity

For the disadvantages, we can list the following:

  • increase in time to build from scratch — you need to setup more things before starting to develop a valuable feature for the client.
  • increase in code — you need more files (classes and interfaces) than in an n-tier architecture.
  • possible loss of optimization — being closer to implementations might grant you better performances. You would lose this in profit of looser coupling which IMHO is a good trade-off.

Editor's Note: Honnestly, reading this again... I don't feel like these are real disadvantages. They can be easily overcome with experience, and will make you gain time on the long run, especially if you decide to work with tests (which you should if you want to produce good code!).

When to use it?​

When you need to develop a complex software, that you want to test your features and want to deliver something valuable that will not increase the buglog once in production. It can also be mixed with methodologies that make it a strong reliability like DDD and TDD.

So why do I prefer CA over N-Tier?​

You might know now but I am tired of developing crappy things, I'm tired of working in a company where you get told to "develop fast and we will improve it later". Later never comes.

I am so tired of such way of working that I fell in love with 3 things:

  1. Clean Architecture, and
  2. Test-Driven Development, and
  3. Software Craftsmanship.

But more seriously, I haven't explained why I like it... In a few words, let me tell you. You need to know that developing an application without tests, it's like developing with your eyes closed: you do mistakes. I then started digging this part of my job I was neglecting at the time: testing. Thanks to my professional experience at Pwc Luxembourg, I met wonderful people who taught me a lot of new things.

That was when I've been asked to write an application following a particular architecture... And everything got solved once I practiced.

Developing with Clean Archi, for me, it is the real culmination of software development where the technical "parts" can finally be changed without having to rework something else. The truth is, I learnt so much with Clean Architecture:

  • I understood the real deal that Dependency Injection represents ;
  • I succeeded in applying SOLID principles better than all the other times I tried, in vain ;
  • I understod that I had to name my interfaces independantly of the implementation that could ensue from it since I could potentially have 3 different implementations of IPdfGenerator ;
  • I understood that testing is fun ;
  • I understood that writing apps without bugs is possible and should be common.

And I went to IT school! They explained what dependency injection, SOLID principles, clean code... are, they taught me how to prepare for a development and avoid the majority of bugs... But that doesn't mean I haven't written horrible code or buggy apps or patched a feature and broken something else in the process.

So, I highly encourage you to learn more about these 3 topics I listed above. The rest should come... They represent what I would love to call the best mindset for the next generation of developers.

I would also recommend to learn more by looking at the following resources:

  • The presentation of Guillherme Ferreira on The Grand Unified Theory of Clean Architecture and Test Pyramid at NDC Porto ;
  • Valentina Cupać's slides about TDD and Clean Architecture driven by behaviour ;
  • A blog post relating an introduction to CA ;
  • The example of such structure that is Jason Taylor's Clean Architecture Template!

Conclusion​

What finally makes the n-tier architecture obsolete is that it is actually data-centric unlike the clean archi that is domain-centric (logic). It took us time to understand that what gives value to our clients is not the data, but the business logic that allows to process that data!

If you are still interested in learning more on the topic, I also happened to stumble upon these online resources:

  • Samuel Oloruntoba's explanations of the SOLID principles ;
  • Mark Seemann's article on the topic of adapters ;
  • Sean G. Wright comment on "Clean architecture - Your approach" ;
  • The meetup group of Software Craftsmanship Luxembourg ;
  • The meetup group of Tech Excellence.

And you, what architecture do you use for your projects?

Stay up to date, subscribe to my newsletter!
